Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Aisha, a 22-year-old South Asian woman and delivery driver, has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic mugging that occurred six months ago. On that day, she was delivering packages in a dimly lit alley when two men approached her, forcing her to hand over her wallet and phone. She felt overwhelmed by the sense of being trapped and helpless, compounded by the presence of one man who seemed to be acting suspiciously. Since then, Aisha has developed strong triggers that evoke intense distress whenever she encounters similar situations. Being forced to do something against her will is particularly distressing for her; even the mere thought of it can lead to a surge of anxiety. The police are another trigger because their presence reminds her of that night's sense of helplessness and vulnerability. The traumatic event has deeply affected Aisha's daily life, especially as a delivery driver. She now avoids driving as much as possible, often opting for public transportation or finding other ways to avoid being alone in her vehicle. This avoidance is rooted in the belief that she will never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened and the persistent feeling of isolation from others who seem unaffected by similar incidents. Aisha has also turned to drug use as a way to cope with her distress, telling herself that the event did not really happen or was not that bad. This magical thinking provides temporary relief but does little to address the underlying issues. The emotional intensity she feels often occurs without clear images, leaving her in a state of heightened anxiety. During moments when Aisha experiences auditory recall of the traumatic event-such as hearing the voices of the men who mugged her-it intensifies her sense of threat. She frequently wakes up during the night to check if she is safe and always identifies escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere, even though she knows these places are safe. The snapshots in her mind that represent moments from the traumatic event exacerbate her feelings of helplessness. Aisha's negative appraisals have significantly influenced her coping mechanisms. She believes she will never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened, leading her to isolate further and avoid situations that remind her of the trauma. Her sense of isolation deepens when she compares herself to others who seem unaffected by similar incidents, which fuels her reliance on drug use and magical thinking. The cycle of distress intensifies as Aisha's memories trigger intense emotions and a heightened sense of threat, leading her to engage in maladaptive strategies such as avoiding driving and using drugs. These behaviors further isolate her from others and reinforce the belief that she cannot stop bad things from happening to her. For example, on one particularly difficult day at work, Aisha encountered a police officer while making deliveries, which immediately triggered intense anxiety. She avoided further interaction by taking an alternate route home but found herself unable to relax even in the safety of her own apartment. This experience left her feeling more isolated and convinced that she cannot control such situations. The combination of these factors has significantly impacted Aisha's work performance and personal relationships. Her avoidance behaviors have led to frequent absences from work, causing tension with her supervisor. She also struggles to maintain connections with friends who do not understand the depth of her distress. Despite her efforts to cope, Aisha is finally seeking help because she feels that the cycle of anxiety and avoidance has become overwhelming. What frightens her most is the constant fear of encountering another situation where she might feel helpless again. However, she also hopes that therapy will provide a way to reclaim control over her life and find peace with what happened. In summary, Aisha's experience after the traumatic mugging has created a self-reinforcing cycle of distress and avoidance, deeply impacting her daily life as a delivery driver. The interplay between her triggers, negative appraisals, memory disturbances, sense of threat, and maladaptive strategies forms a complex network that tightens around her with each encounter.
